title: A Inheritance for the Witness
premise: Retired detective Xanthe Kavanagh receives two letters the same morning: one confessing to a thirty-year-old murder he witnessed as a child, and one promising him his late mother's estate if he can name her killer within six weeks. As he reopens the cold case, Xanthe realizes the confessor knows the original file better than any investigator ever did, feeding him truths laced with lies. The trail leads back to the coastal village that erased its own history, where survival was bought with silence. In the end, Xanthe discovers the letters came from the killer's own child, who has spent a lifetime watching him; he names the murderer at last, claims the inheritance, and chooses to burn the confession rather than let belonging be bought twice.
about_author: Oscar Ravensworth is the pen name of a former archivist who spent two decades cataloguing unsolved case files before turning to fiction. They write quiet mysteries about people haunted by paperwork, and live in a seaside town they refuse to name.

chapters.title: Two Envelopes
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. On a rain-slicked Tuesday, two letters arrive at Kavanagh's Books: one unsigned confession to the 1994 murder of Maren Kavanagh, one from a solicitor promising an inheritance if Xanthe identifies her killer in six weeks. The emotional beat is dread disguised as curiosity—the past knocking on a door he bricked over.

chapters.title: The Shop That Keeps Him
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. We see his failing bookshop, his routines of invisibility, and his pride: every case taken, closed. His assistant Priya notices the letters have shaken him. He decides, against instinct, to take this one. Emotional beat: stubbornness as armor.

chapters.title: What the File Never Said
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. He requests the original case file and finds pages missing—precisely the pages describing the witness statement of a nine-year-old boy. Someone has been inside the archive recently. Beat: the hunter realizes he is also being hunted.

chapters.title: The Confessor Writes Again
chapters.summary: Interleaved POV: the anonymous letter-writer describes the murder scene with details never made public, then corrects a small error Xanthe noticed—a trap or a gift? Xanthe tests the writer by planting a false detail. Beat: first move in a chess game with a ghost.

chapters.title: Saltmere-on-Sea
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. He returns to the village of his childhood, now gentrified and amnesiac. Old neighbors greet him warmly and lie fluently. He learns his mother worked at Harrow House, the estate now tied to his inheritance. Beat: belonging revealed as performance.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Watched
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, young Xanthe's POV. 1994: the night through a child's eyes—shadows on the boathouse wall, his mother's coat, a voice he almost recognized. Beat: terror rendered tender, establishing what he actually saw versus what he told police.

chapters.title: Harrow House
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. He visits the decaying estate and meets Edith Vane, the elderly housekeeper who remembers everything and admits nothing. She hints his mother knew something worth killing for. Beat: the inheritance begins to feel like bait.

chapters.title: The False Detail Bites
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The confessor's next letter incorporates Xanthe's planted falsehood—meaning the writer is not working from memory alone but from the file itself, and is correcting it. Xanthe narrows suspects to those with archive access. Beat: intellectual thrill, the detective waking up.

chapters.title: Priya Asks Questions
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Worried about Xanthe, she investigates his past and finds the sealed juvenile witness record—and a second name redacted beside his own. Beat: loyalty strained by discovery; the reader learns Xanthe wasn't the only witness.

chapters.title: A Death in the Family of Strangers
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Edith Vane is found dead days after their conversation, staged as a fall. The timing is unmistakable: someone is closing mouths ahead of him. Beat: grief and guilt—the price of asking questions.

chapters.title: The Solicitor's Silence
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The solicitor's office has burned down overnight. The inheritance letter is now untraceable paper. Xanthe realizes the six-week deadline was never legal—it was narrative, someone scripting his investigation. Beat: vertigo; the rules were never real.

chapters.title: What Maren Knew
chapters.summary: Edith's posthumous letter, arranged before her death, reaches Xanthe. His mother had discovered embezzlement and worse at Harrow House—children quietly disappeared from its 'care.' She died because she was going to talk. Beat: righteous fury replacing fear.

chapters.title: The Second Witness
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Following Priya's lead, he finds Tomas Reyes, the other child witness, living rough and terrified. Tomas saw the killer's face and has spent thirty years being paid to forget. Beat: pity and recognition—two survivors, two prices paid.

chapters.title: Tomas Breaks
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Tomas describes the man at the boathouse: someone trusted, official, wearing the village's goodwill like a uniform. Before he can name him, Tomas's caravan burns. He survives, barely. Beat: escalation—the killer stops being careful.

chapters.title: The Archive Ghost
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. He stakes out the county records office and catches the intruder: a middle-aged woman, Ruth Calloway, daughter of the retired police superintendent who ran the 1994 investigation—and buried it. Beat: revelation reframes everything; the confessor is the killer's child.

chapters.title: Ruth's Confession
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. She confesses she found her father's private files years ago, learned he protected the killer to protect the town's money, and has been using Xanthe to finish what justice couldn't. But she swears her father isn't the killer—he was shielding someone else. Beat: betrayal braided with alliance.

chapters.title: The Name Beneath the Name
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Cross-referencing Ruth's files with his mother's notes hidden in a hollowed book in his own shop all along, he finds the pattern: the man who signed off on Harrow House 'placements'—now the village's beloved patriarch, Aldous Crane. Beat: cold clarity; the trap designs itself.

chapters.title: Deadline Week
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. With three days left, Xanthe publicly announces he'll name the killer at a village assembly, forcing Crane's hand. Crane offers him the estate outright to stay silent—the inheritance as muzzle. Beat: temptation offered plainly; the theme made flesh.

chapters.title: Boathouse, Again
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Crane lures him to the boathouse at night to finish what 1994 started. Xanthe goes knowingly, wired with Ruth's recording equipment, walking into the dark he fled as a boy. Beat: fear mastered, not absent—the novel's emotional summit approaches.

chapters.title: The Witness Speaks
chapters.summary: Climax, Xanthe's POV. Crane confesses in full, believing Xanthe alone and cornered; the recording captures everything, including the threat on his life. Priya and Ruth intervene as Crane turns violent. Xanthe finally says aloud what the nine-year-old couldn't: I saw you. Beat: catharsis through testimony.

chapters.title: Probate
chapters.summary: Falling action, mixed POV. Crane is arrested; the town's complicity surfaces in headlines. Xanthe inherits Harrow House and finds it worthless except as evidence—and as a place the disappeared children might finally be remembered. Beat: justice without triumph.

chapters.title: Ashes and First Editions
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. He burns the confession copy Ruth kept, denying the killer's story a future, and converts Harrow House into a memorial library run with Priya. The bookshop survives on new foot traffic. Final beat: belonging chosen, not inherited—the price of survival finally paid forward.
